sources.title: Northwest Coast Hall: Pacific Northwest Nations
sources.note: Community-curated museum overview distinguishing living Northwest Coast Nations, territories, languages, knowledge, objects and cultural persistence.

sources.title: Prehistoric Inhabitants of the Olympic Peninsula
sources.note: National Park Service archaeological sequence showing changing local marine foods, salmon reliance, tools, houses and regional variation.

sources.title: Kiix̣in Village and Fortress National Historic Site
sources.note: Parks Canada evidence for nearly three thousand years of Huu-ay-aht occupation, houses, middens, trade and later defensive architecture.

sources.title: Historical Coast Salish Art
sources.note: Burke Museum dates for Hoko River basketry, Wapato Creek hat and other localized Coast Salish material histories.

sources.title: Coast Salish Weaving Tools and Technologies
sources.note: Burke Museum guide to later documented coiling, twining, plaiting, fibre preparation, cooking baskets and living innovation.

sources.title: Tlingit Archeology, Legends, and Oral Histories at Sitka National Historical Park
sources.note: National Park Service excavations, radiocarbon dates, hearth, probable structure, cache pits and dated limits on spruce-pitch evidence.

sources.title: Shis’g’i Noow, the Tlingit Fortified Village
sources.note: National Park Service synthesis of local Tlingit fish weirs, seasonal camps, cache pits, salmon relationships and later conflict.

sources.title: Nang X̲aldangaas
sources.note: Council of the Haida Nation account of foods, villages, archaeology, canoe travel, trade, relationships and present stewardship.

sources.title: Nuxalk Territory Maps
sources.note: Nuxalk Nation account of multiple villages, family ancestry, crests, songs, governance and continuing occupation of Nuxalk territory.

sources.title: Nuxalkmc: The Nuxalk People
sources.note: Nuxalk Nation account of colonial schooling, family and language continuity, community education and younger generations learning on ancestral sites.

sources.title: 3500 Years of Shellfish Mariculture on the Northwest Coast of North America
sources.note: Peer-reviewed dating of northern Quadra Island clam gardens, construction methods, preservation problems and long-lived marine management.

sources.title: Fish Traps as Evidence of Changing Social Cooperation and Investment on the Pacific Northwest Coast
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis of 511 radiocarbon dates connecting local wooden fish traps with cooperation, settlements, houses and change.

sources.title: Indigenous Sex-Selective Salmon Harvesting in Burrard Inlet
sources.note: Peer-reviewed ancient-DNA study of dated salmon bones from four Tsleil-Waututh ancestral settlements and selective harvesting evidence.

sources.title: Chumash Midden
sources.note: National Park Service evidence for dated island visits, middens, fish and shell remains, plank canoes, shell-bead production and exchange.

sources.title: Original People of California’s Historical Use of Native Plants
sources.note: University of California account of locally documented plant foods, acorn leaching, medicine, shelter, clothing, tools and basketry.

sources.title: The Miwok People
sources.note: California State Parks account of Miwok acorn storage and processing, cooking baskets, bark shelters and local cultural landscapes.

sources.title: Native People of the Mendocino Coast
sources.note: California State Parks account of Northern Pomo seasonal movement, redwood use, women’s basketry and living descendants maintaining practice.

sources.title: Makah Museum and Ozette Archaeological Site
sources.note: Makah Tribe account of community-held Ozette archaeology, preserved whaling and fishing gear, basketry, longhouse and canoe evidence.

sources.title: Makah Canoeing
sources.note: Makah Tribe account of varied canoe sizes, children’s practice canoes, manufacture, repairs, navigation knowledge and current journeys.

sources.title: Makah Whaling
sources.note: Makah Tribe account of two-thousand-year-old local whale bones and harpoon barbs, specialized gear, teamwork and modern continuity.

sources.title: Makah Tribe History
sources.note: Makah Tribe account of specific villages, extended-family cedar houses, seasonal camps, foods, marine knowledge and living practice.

sources.title: Chumash Culture
sources.note: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians account of living culture, children’s programs, basketry, Samala teaching and renewed tomol crossings.

sources.title: Chinook Indian Nation: Unbroken Canoe Culture
sources.note: Chinook Indian Nation account of continuing community, canoe work, salmon ceremony, language renewal and present recognition struggle.

sources.title: The Cultural Landscape of Fort Vancouver: Indian Country, Pre-1824
sources.note: National Park Service synthesis of lower Columbia villages, seasonal land use, plant tending, trade routes and evidence limitations.

sources.title: Ethnohistorical Overview of the Middle Columbia River
sources.note: National Park Service study of later documented lower Columbia raiding, captivity, slavery, social position and regional differences.

sources.title: Why Were Petroglyphs, Pictographs, and Inscriptions Made?
sources.note: National Park Service distinction among rock markings and inscriptions, possible meanings, living cultural knowledge and interpretive uncertainty.

sources.title: New Plan Charts Path for Eulachon Recovery
sources.note: NOAA account of eulachon biology, candlefish nickname, seasonal importance, grease trade routes, current fisheries and conservation threats.

sources.title: First Peoples’ Language Map of British Columbia
sources.note: First Peoples’ Cultural Council explanation of distinct languages and families, community perspectives, mapping limits and language revitalization.

sources.title: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians History
sources.note: Tribal account distinguishing ancient Chumash life, oral transmission, Spanish mission violence, population loss and modern cultural survival.

sources.title: Coast Salish
sources.note: Community-curated museum account of more than forty independent Nations, over twenty related languages, local objects and living continuity.

proposedOverrides.summary: A broad atlas umbrella corrected through local Indigenous and archaeological evidence.

batchIdentityNotes: The atlas phrase is treated as a broad editorial economy umbrella, never one people, nation, language, government, border or uniform culture.
Every exact feature is counted: 25 snapshots have four-part MultiPolygons and the 1500 snapshot has a contracted three-part MultiPolygon.
The 800 southern contraction, 1492 named-layer gap, 1500 northern return and 1530 disappearance are taxonomy seams, not population events.
Named Nations, archaeological sites and historical comparisons remain localized and dated. No practice is generalized across the whole Pacific footprint without evidence.
Living Indigenous Nations and community institutions are explicit; the 1530 endpoint is not extinction and no inferred successor genealogy is created.

No contemporaneous writing sample is supplied because none is securely attributable to the umbrella and interval. Rock markings are not recast as phonetic script, and modern orthographies are not borrowed.
